On the Couch with Leslie Bibb

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since appearing in season three of HBO’s The White Lotus in 2025, American actress Leslie Bibb has had no problem keeping busy.
  • Outside her day job, Bibb also happens to be a design enthusiast—she’s at the moment renovating the upstate Fresh York home that she shares with longtime partner, fellow actor Sam Rockwell.
  • Sources indicate that next up for Bibb is a starring role alongside Brett Goldstein in Amazon Prime series Escorted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since appearing in season three of HBO’s The White Lotus in 2025, American actress Leslie Bibb has had no problem keeping busy. The North Dakota-born, Virginia-raised actress already had screen credits spanning from the Iron Man films to Apple TV+’s Palm Royale, but Bibb’s performance on Mike White’s hit series as one-third of a slightly toxic friendship trio spotlighted the actress’s knack for blending comedy and drama. Not to mention, her blunt bob served as hair inspiration for the masses. After The White Lotus, Bibb went on to guest star on HBO’s Hacks, landing her an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy.

Outside her day job, Bibb also happens to be a design enthusiast—she’s at the moment renovating the upstate Fresh York home that she shares with longtime partner, fellow actor Sam Rockwell. For the interiors, Bibb has teamed up with ELLE Decor A-List designer Shawn Henderson, who often pops up on Bibb’s Instagram account, attending birthday parties and surveying the concrete shell that will one day be a pool. In the kitchen, Bibb is partnering with LG Signature on appliances that gel with the new renovation.

Sources indicate that next up for Bibb is a starring role alongside Brett Goldstein in Amazon Prime series Escorted. She is also executive producing a show with HBO called The Rush Whisperer, a dark comedy about sorority rush. Together with the home renovation, she has trouble choosing what to highlight. “I’m just grateful that I’m able to juggle work and life and my relationship with Sam,” says the actress. For our On the Couch survey, she shares her greatest design inspirations, entertaining tips, and the artists that have her heart.

Sources indicate that favorite Eras of Design: All of them... well, most of them. I'm not into cold, modern pieces from the 1980s or that shabby chic stuff. But I do like a house that isn't just one thing, that is a mix of eras and has warmth—a house that is inviting and notes, “Come in, kick off your shoes, grab a drink and let's hang out.” And I love color.

Favorite Sofa: I don't have a favorite sofa, but I do love an L-shaped sofa for watching TV so Sammy and I can be together but also have our own spaces to sprawl out.

Industry observers note that maverick design style trick: I feel incredibly lucky to have my friend and fabulous interior designer, Shawn Henderson, as my secret weapon. Home renovations can be a nightmare, but having Shawn as my partner in crime has really made the experience so much fun. And let's be honest, the kitchen is the heart of any home. When I think of LG Signature, I think about how they design to honor your lifestyle rather than compete with it.

In a recent development, most beloved buildings: I love the Chrysler Building. It always takes my breath away. Also, there is a church where my parents are buried in the country and I just love it. It is so small and quaint and the view from its windows and the grounds just make me smile.

Destination Museum: Musée d'Orsay because I get to see my favorite painting by Gustave Caillebotte called The Floor Scrapers. Honestly, wandering through museums or art galleries is one of my happy places so in any city you will find me making a pit stop to get an art fix and steal some inspo. I just saw the Krasner and Pollock "Past Continuous" exhibit at the Met and it blew my socks off.

Go-to gallery or galleries: Any gallery, anywhere. Just go in and see what people are making. It will always inspire you in some way.

Favorite Artist/Artwork: I love art and wandering around a museum or gallery is one of my safe spaces. I am mesmerized by pieces from Noah Davis. I love Helen Frankenthaler and Hilma af Klint. Also, I love Nick Cave and Danny Fox and Ramon Enrich and Peter Doig. The photographs from Sally Mann I love, too. Honestly, there are so many. I am in awe.

Favorite getaway: Staycation...and hopefully at our home upstate once we are done!

Best Host/Hostess Gift: I love to wrap a bottle of olive oil in a great kitchen towel so it is two gifts in one. I like a gift that can be put to use.

Entertaining Tips: Always have a well-stocked bar with loads of options and feed your guests. Also, make sure you have a killer dance mix going because it ain't a party unless people start dancing. And if you have more than 25 people, hire a bartender. Otherwise you won't get to socialize and you will be just hosting all night and you will be exhausted.

Recent findings suggest that cocktail or Mocktail of Choice: I am obsessed with this nonalcoholic Kolsch beer by Best Day Brewing Company. And winter is upon us, so a great martini. I am in Italy right now and am besotted with Negronis.

Watch to Wear: There are two I really love: one I own that Sam gave me so long ago, my Rolex, and the other is one I want to get, which is the Cartier Baignoire.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

Industry observers note that you can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

According to recent reports, while you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

#20251. Breaking: What Is Unrequited Love? Experts Explain Why It Hurts So Much and How to Move On

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1287 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cosmopolitan ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: What Is Unrequited Love? Experts Explain Why It Hurts So Much and How to Move On

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there's nothing quite like having feelings for someone who doesn't feel the same way.
  • Recent findings suggest that welcome to the deeply frustrating world of unrequited love.
  • And just because your feelings aren't mutual doesn't mean they're any less real or painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there's nothing quite like having feelings for someone who doesn't feel the same way. Maybe it's a friend you've secretly been into for years, an ex you can't seem to get over, or someone who keeps giving you just enough attention to convince yourself there's still a chance. And while you know, logically, that you can't make someone fall in love with you, that doesn't stop you from overanalyzing every text, replaying every interaction, and wondering whether things might eventually change.

Recent findings suggest that welcome to the deeply frustrating world of unrequited love. “At its core, unrequited love is a love that’s not reciprocated from one person to another,” explains Leanna Stockard, LMFT, a marriage and family therapist with LifeStance Health. “One person either has stronger feelings for the other or there is no feeling at all from the other.”.

And just because your feelings aren't mutual doesn't mean they're any less real or painful. In fact, clinical psychologist Monica Vermani, PsyD, says unrequited love can cause “tremendous emotional turmoil,” leaving you feeling anxious, stressed, or questioning your self-worth.

It has been revealed that so, how can you tell if you're experiencing unrequited love versus a particularly intense crush? And how do you move on when part of you is still holding out hope? Here's what experts want you to know about recognizing unrequited love, understanding why it happens, and figuring out what to do next.

Essentially, unrequited love looks like an imbalance of effort, affection, and attention. Stockard states some signs your feelings might not be reciprocated include the other person consistently taking a long time to respond to your texts or calls, avoiding spending time with you, or, in some cases, not even knowing who you are.

Unrequited love often happens between friends, when one person starts developing romantic feelings while the other sees the relationship as strictly platonic. It can also happen when you fall for someone who's unavailable, whether that's someone already in a relationship, an ex, a person who lives far away, an authority figure, or even a celebrity.

If you're wondering whether your feelings are one-sided, here are some signs Vermani claims to look out for:.

Vermani says unrequited love can sometimes have more to do with our own expectations and unmet emotional needs than the person we're actually falling for.

“Unrequited love is often based on pursuing from a romantic partner what is lacking in our own lives,” she explains. “The reality of this quest for love as a means of filling in the gaps or deficits in our lives (and ourselves) is that it comes from a place of lack. When we set our sights on an ‘ideal’ partner who ticks all the boxes on our must-have list, we often create the ideal conditions for unrequited love.”.

Recent findings suggest that think about it: When you're convinced someone is your perfect match, it's easy to start imagining what your life together could look like, even if the relationship itself doesn't actually exist. You might find yourself focusing on their best qualities, overlooking signs they're not interested, or holding onto the idea that everything would fall into place if they just felt the same way. And sometimes, that imagined relationship can feel easier to hold onto than dealing with the uncertainty and vulnerability of a real one.

“Many of us are brought up to believe that to be happy and fulfilled in life, we need someone—the one—to complete us,” Vermani indicates. “The main reason we suffer, though, is that we don’t accept people as they are, or accept situations as they are.”.

Of course, it's also possible to develop strong feelings for someone without knowing them on a deeper level. You might know their favorite food, birthday, and practically every detail of their Instagram activity, but that doesn't necessarily mean you know what they'd be like as a romantic partner. And even if you're close friends, the intimacy you share isn't necessarily the same as a mutual romantic connection.

The short answer? Your feelings can absolutely be real, even if they're not reciprocated. But there's a difference between loving someone and being in a loving relationship with them. Sometimes, what feels like love can also be a combination of intense longing, attraction, and the idea of what a relationship with that person could look like. And if you don't know them on a deeper level, you might be falling for a version of them that doesn't entirely match reality.

“When love is mutual, there’s balance, give and take, shared intimacy, trust, mutual transparency (meaning a lack of secrecy), and commitment that grows over time,” explains Vermani.

Recent findings suggest that unrequited love is a pretty common experience, especially when you're still figuring out what traits you value in a potential partner. And having feelings for someone who doesn't feel the same way isn't inherently unhealthy. It becomes more concerning when those feelings start affecting your well-being, preventing you from pursuing other relationships, or making it difficult to respect the other person's boundaries.

Sources indicate that “Being in a one-sided relationship may lead to further feelings of rejection and increased anxiety,” Stockard notes. And while it's normal to have a hard time letting go, continually holding out hope for a relationship that isn't going to happen can make moving forward even harder. “Unrequited love can be dangerous when a person takes their love to a level such as stalking, manipulation, or other dangerous forms of obsession,” she adds.

That stated, not every case of unrequited love turns into something unhealthy. It's entirely possible to care about someone, accept that they don't feel the same way, and eventually move forward without those feelings interfering with your life or theirs.

In a recent development, just because someone doesn't return your feelings doesn't mean you can magically turn yours off. But if the situation is causing you anxiety or heartbreak, finding ways to refocus your energy can help. After all, continuing to pursue someone who's made it clear they're not interested is only going to make moving on harder.

Sources indicate that stockard claims there are a few different approaches you can try, starting with giving yourself some space. “Determine if you need time away from the other person to gain clarity, and respect their needs as well,” she suggests. “As much as your feelings for them are valid, their feelings of not wanting to pursue something further with you are also valid.” That might mean resisting the urge to text them, making looks that don't revolve around them, or limiting contact until your feelings have lessened or gone away.

It has been revealed that if you're still struggling, Stockard also recommends seeking therapy. “This process can help you feel confident that a partner who values you and wants you exists, and lessen the fixation on someone who does not,” she explains. Therapy can also help you better understand your relationship patterns and what you're looking for in a partner.

Industry observers note that and while it might not feel like it right now, time and perspective can make a difference. “Often unrequited love is a fantasy—an intense, entirely one-sided romantic infatuation—rather than actual love. Over time, infatuations fade and neutralize,” Vermani claims. “It’s important to focus on self-love, self-care, and self-fulfillment, because when we’re content with ourselves, we’re able to walk away from unrequited love that’s not in our highest and best interest. Once that happens, we’re able to recognize and find reciprocal love.”.

Sources indicate that you don't have to stop caring about someone overnight. But you can start making choices that leave room for a relationship where your feelings are actually returned.

#20247. Latest Update: The Slow Fade Might Actually Be Worse Than Ghosting

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cosmopolitan ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The Slow Fade Might Actually Be Worse Than Ghosting

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love.
  • According to recent reports, no one likes being rejected—unless, of course, it’s some kind of kink...in which case, more power to you.
  • According to recent reports, and while I’m not going to sit here and advocate for ghosting either—in fact, quite the opposite!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

According to recent reports, no one likes being rejected—unless, of course, it’s some kind of kink...in which case, more power to you. But that one-two punch to the gut is only made worse when the person you’re dating doesn’t even give you the common courtesy of honest communication.

According to recent reports, and while I’m not going to sit here and advocate for ghosting either—in fact, quite the opposite! We’re all about the anti-ghosting movement—at least the silence provides an answer of sorts, unlike the mind fuck that is the slow fade (aka the fizzle). Unless you’re in a happy, stable relationship (heard of those?) and not dealing with the same complex dating landscape as the rest of us, you’ve likely endured this form of emotional warfare at least once. The texts come fewer and farther between, they’ve stopped initiating plans, and their responses are as stale as week-old bread. It’s a pattern of mixed communication that can lead to a lot of second-guessing.

According to recent reports, and though we may hate to admit it to ourselves (a little delusion is fine, right? Don’t tell my therapist I mentioned that), your situationship/casual fling/almost significant other is probably not “drowning in work” or whatever other half-assed excuse they gave you last. It’s more likely they’re just not that into you and don’t have the courage, respect, and ahem, balls to admit it.

According to recent reports, and while you—and I, and literally any living, breathing human being—deserve a whole lot more than some emotionally incompetent clown who resorts to this form of immaturity, that doesn’t mean the slow fade isn’t hurtful and difficult to move on from. Without a concrete breakup or explanation as to what went wrong, there’s a lot of room for confusion.

“It’s much more brutal for the person on the receiving end because it leaves them with mixed signals. Rather than having information outright, they’re left to wonder what the other person is thinking, which can cause stress and anxiety and prevent them from moving on,” says licensed marriage and family therapist Emily Simonian, head of clinical learning for Thriveworks.

It’s no small epidemic either. Ghosting’s passive-aggressive cousin (as Hinge dubbed it) has become a familiar post-date communication matter for singles. According to the app’s 2023 LGBTQIA+ DATE Report, 90 percent of those surveyed said they were worried about someone “fizzling,” or slow-fading them, and it’s not just an issue in the LGBTQIA+ community. Another study by Superdrug Online Doctor found that 63 percent of participants admitted to slow-fading someone themselves. Cool cool cool.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s become rampant in dating culture in response to the idea that ghosting is inappropriate or lacks compassion,” Simonian says. “However, the same individuals who might ghost due to lack of communication skills have just found a upcoming way to avoid having difficult conversations while distancing themselves from the negative associations of ghosting.”.

So while, yay, good, everyone’s finally getting the message that ghosting is not okay, the slow fade is no better. In fact, some (cough, cough me and the actual licensed therapist here) might even call it worse. It breeds confusion and, as Simonian puts it, “perpetuates the trend of avoiding difficult yet honest conversations in the dating space.” And having those difficult but honest conversations is a valuable skill you’ll need in order to make a relationship work when you’re ready. If you're the slow-fader, these negative communication habits won't exactly serve you in the long run. And they can be really destructive for the person on the receiving end, since being strung along and fed mixed messages can inspire distrust with future partners.

It has been revealed that so what do we do to survive this hurtful dating pattern—other than the occasional, healthy cry and regular therapy? Well, for starters, if you’ve participated in the slow fade (or “fizzling,” as it’s also commonly referred to) in the past, it’s time to try a different—ahem, more mature—strategy when ending things with someone.

“The best approach is always compassionate honesty,” Simonian claims. “Lead with something positive when you’re having these tough conversations, but be direct. It might be harder to let someone down directly, but it is the most compassionate way to end things.”.

Industry observers note that TL;DR: Be kind and be honest, because choosing anything but that approach is only going to make things more difficult for all parties involved. And while you can’t control another person’s actions—and as a result, you also can’t necessarily avoid the dreaded slow fade from happening to you—you can be accountable for not creating that confusion on your own end.

If your situationship is too chicken to have a real convo and is instead offering lame one-word replies, you can initiate a chat instead of just enduring (read: crying into a pint of Ben & Jerry’s) the energy shift.

“There isn’t really a way to avoid getting slow-faded,” Simonian adds. “However, you can take control of the situation and ask directly whether or not the person wants to continue dating to avoid being left in limbo.”.

In other words, use the maturity they couldn’t muster to pull yourself out of the gray area. You deserve clarity, and they deserve to stew in their own discomfort for attempting to slow-fade you in the first place. Hey, a good ol’ fashioned dumping is timeless. Let’s bring that back and stop with this immature, indirect approach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holiday decorating is supposed to be a joyous event, but picking the right tree can be surprisingly complicated.
  • The truth is, any tree can be beautiful in the right setting, so if you’re feeling unsure about which one fits your home, we’ve created the ultimate guide on which tree is right for your holiday centerpiece.
  • Sources indicate that the Fraser fir is one of the most popular types of Christmas tree, especially for households east of the Rocky Mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holiday decorating is supposed to be a joyous event, but picking the right tree can be surprisingly complicated. There’s a lot of height, circumference, and branch density variation—some people like a full, fluffy look, while others opt for a more minimal tree—and don’t even entice us with the real versus faux debate.

The truth is, any tree can be beautiful in the right setting, so if you’re feeling unsure about which one fits your home, we’ve created the ultimate guide on which tree is right for your holiday centerpiece. Ahead, we're sharing the most popular types of Christmas trees for every household.

Additional copy by Alyssa Khan.

Sources indicate that the Fraser fir is one of the most popular types of Christmas tree, especially for households east of the Rocky Mountains. Firs, in general, are some of the most common trees grown for the holiday season, notes Ward Dilmore, founder of Petrus Landscaping in California. There's a good reason for this: They have a perfect balance of deep green color and even, stiff branching, he says, which makes them a breeze to decorate.

Canaan fir trees often get compared to Fraser and balsam firs, thanks to their similar growing patterns and branch density, but this variety has a major benefit above the rest: needle retention. It sheds less than other firs, which means less cleanup for you.

Most Voluminous: Eastern White Pine.

Often a home for many birds, including woodpeckers, the eastern white pine is fluffy and fast-growing. With foliage that's thin, delicate, and silvery-green, this tree is best paired with lightweight ornaments and minimal decorations.

Industry observers note that A classic type of Christmas tree, the noble fir is native to the Cascade and Pacific Coast mountain ranges of the Northwestern United States. With strong branches, this tree ensures your precious family heirlooms won't be at risk of falling, and the long peak is ideal for an oversized tree topper.

Longest-Lasting: Arizona Cypress.

The Arizona cypress is the most drought-tolerant evergreen out there—with the right care, this type of Christmas tree can last longer than other evergreens. With its thick, layered branches and lacy silver-blue foliage, this tree is a beautiful alternative to the silver fir.

Best for Outdoors: Leyland Cypress.

Recent findings suggest that fast-growing and cone-like in shape, Leyland cypresses are more frequently used as privacy plantings rather than as Christmas trees. However, this richly colored cypress tree grows almost everywhere in the United States, except for the most northern parts of the Dakotas, Michigan, and Montana. If you have one in your yard, why not string lights on it?

Thickest Coverage: Virginia Pine.

You’ll find this bushy type of Christmas tree primarily in Southern states, according to the Real Christmas Tree Board. Thanks to its stout branches, it should have no problem holding up your heaviest ceramic ornaments. It also has a piney fragrance and keeps its needles well throughout the season, as long as you give it plenty of water to drink.

Industry observers note that also known as a red fir, these striking trees are one of the rarest types of Christmas trees, notes horticulturist and botanical designer Nathan Heinrich. They're slow-growing, and only a few farmers and harvesters have permits in California and Oregon to harvest them in the wild each year, he explains. "The reason these trees make such perfect Christmas trees is because they have such perfectly spaced, open, elegant branches that make hanging ornaments and lights easy," Heinrich says.

Like Miracle on 34th Street and peppermint hot chocolate, the balsam fir is a holiday classic. It's also the most fragrant of all types of Christmas trees, according to the Real Christmas Tree Board. You can find these at Christmas tree farms in Canada, Upcoming England, the upper Great Lakes, and Pennsylvania, along with lots of retail locations east of the Rocky Mountains.

The Scotch pine often flies under the radar, but it's a designer-favorite Christmas tree choice, and it has great needle retention. "With vibrant green and durable needles that resist shedding, it's low maintenance," notes Newly introduced York designer Artem Kropovinsky of interior design studio Arsight. "Its robust branches accommodate even the heaviest ornaments, and its dense appearance gives rooms a fuller, festive look.".

Industry observers note that the trees you see in lots often have been pruned and sheared into the quintessential Christmas tree shape, explains Lisa Tadewaldt, an ISA-certified arborist and owner of Portland, Oregon–based Urban Forest Professionals. She recommends getting a permit and cutting a tree that's native to your area down in the forest. In the Pacific Northwest, her favorite tree in its natural form is a grand fir. "It is going to give more Charlie Brown vibes than Hallmark Christmas vibes, but it has a flat needle pattern that gives it an air of elegance that balances out the thinner, more homespun branching pattern," she notes.

It has been revealed that with its signature bluish needles, the robust blue spruce has a full, triangular shape, indicates Kropovinsky. "Apart from its signature color, this tree releases a fresh scent similar to frosty woodlands," he says. Bonus for pet owners: "Given the tree's pointed foliage, pets often steer clear of it.".

Best for Lights: Eastern Red Cedar.

With its flexible needles and twigs, the Eastern red cedar doesn't hold ornaments all that well. But don’t let that deter you! If your heart is set on this hardy juniper, it looks great draped with lights, says ISA-certified master arborist Blake Watkins, operations partner at Monster Tree Service.

The Douglas fir is a type of Christmas tree that is synonymous with the Pacific Northwest, but is available at holiday tree markets nationwide. It's also one of the more affordable types of Christmas trees you can find. "Dark green foliage and hanging needles make this tree gorgeous even without ornaments," Watkins says.

The concolor fir (also called the white fir) is the type of tree you'd like to sidle up next to with a mug of mulled wine. While many trees have pine scents, this one actually gives off a citrus aroma that has garnered it some devoted fans, according to the Michigan State University Extension. Looks-wise, its branches have long, silvery, bluish-green needles.

Before becoming a home writer, Meghan worked in the fashion industry for two years, writing for Harper's Bazaar after graduating from Iowa State University with a bachelor's degree in apparel merchandising. When she's not interviewing interior designers about home trends, you can find Meghan reading a fictional thriller with her cat in her lap, planning themed parties, or strolling through flea markets searching for chunky candle holders and vintage bookends.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It has been revealed that pajamas have officially left the bedroom and entered the party circuit. Soft, slouchy, chic, easy-to-wear pieces are everywhere on the recent runways. And some of the most interesting examples also come with a strong, literal interpretation of pajama dressing. But even for those who aren’t as daring, the runways are filled with slips, pajama-inspired tops, robe coats, blouses, and lingerie undone dressing. Luckily, fashion’s pajama fascination comes at the perfect time for occasion dressing season.

For fall/winter 2026, Sandy Liang’s jackets were refashioned from bedspreads and silky pajama tops were reinvented with major ruffles, then turned into dresses. The point of reference was a cross between Marie Antoinette and Kiki’s Delivery Service. Elsewhere, Ashley Williams sent out models wearing dresses with silky bed appliqués inspired by ’80s bedrooms and childhood furniture. Marie Adam-Leenaerdt showed neon reversible robe jackets and hot pink lace sets inspired by the kind of slips one might normally use as underpinnings or wear to sleep. “This season is about making with care. About transforming what already exists. About allowing imperfection. More attention,” stated the show notes.

What these looks all also have in common is that they feel like a latest kind of pajama dressing through the female gaze.

In a recent development, the aforementioned pieces make a strong case for statement dressing on their own, with little styling needed. But if you want to go in a different direction, there is also ample inspiration from the fall/winter 2026 collections. But even the humble pajama top has its place in partywear today. It’s impossible not to notice the many silky, vintage-inspired blouses that pull from the everyday roots of the pajama shirt. Dressed up in vibrant shades of turquoise or trimmed in feathers and paired with It shoes and a statement coat, a pajama top is party-ready even with a pair of jeans.

Recent findings suggest that designers clearly agree: At Dior’s spring/summer 2027 show, models walked the runway in soft striped blouses that mirrored the classic pajama shirt, redone with pizazz. With relaxed silhouettes, they were styled with rounded jackets worn open, then paired with wildly patterned bell-shaped skirts or metallic-textured pants. #20233. Why We Need to Stop Saying “I’m Sorry” When Someone Breaks Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1455 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cosmopolitan ↗ Open Full Page

Why We Need to Stop Saying “I’m Sorry” When Someone Breaks Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love.
  • When my last relationship ended, I felt better than I had in months—maybe even years.
  • According to recent reports, it’s not like I’d planned or even expected this post-breakup bliss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

When my last relationship ended, I felt better than I had in months—maybe even years. If I’m being honest, I was probably happier after we split than I was when we first got together, and it made me feel like the heartless Bachelor villain of my own love life.

According to recent reports, it’s not like I’d planned or even expected this post-breakup bliss. Like literally every other person who has ever been in a relationship, I wasn’t exactly looking forward to the end of mine. But when it finally happened, I was relieved—dare I say, excited? It wasn’t even like I had been actively miserable in the relationship; to this day, I’m not even sure whether it’s fair to say it exceeded standard toxicity levels. But I did know it had run its course, and I was grateful to have my future back, one I wouldn’t have to spend trying to convince myself a good-enough relationship was, in fact, good enough.

Recent findings suggest that but to the rest of the world, this largely painless ending appeared to be a tragedy. Anyone I mentioned the split to, from friends and family to random strangers and acquaintances, immediately responded with some version of “I’m sorry.” In response, I’d find myself explaining that actually I was fine and the breakup was very much for the best. Unfortunately, this had a way of making me come off like a heartbroken caricature of a delusional woman desperately trying to convince everyone she’s fine when really I…actually was fine!

According to recent reports, being on the receiving end of all these condolences had me wondering if I actually was delusional—or maybe just dead inside. Had one too many heartbreaks, ghostings, and life-altering situationships rendered me fully incapable of mourning my own relationship the way everyone else seemed to be doing?

Exhausted from absorbing all this well-intentioned, if unsolicited, sympathy, I started trying to avoid mentioning the breakup altogether. Until one day, a few weeks after the split, when I casually broke the news to a friend at a party and she mentioned, “Congratulations!”.

Industry observers note that I was so thrilled, so relieved to finally get a response from someone that actually matched my own feelings, I could’ve wept tears of actual joy. Maybe my lack of grief and I weren’t the problem! Maybe the problem I kept brushing up against with every unsolicited “sorry” had more to do with the patriarchal ideals our society still upholds but which I had recently rejected—the ones that dictate that being partnered, however happily or unhappily, is always superior to being single, especially if you’re a woman.

To be clear, I’m not saying that expressing sympathy for what may very well be an emotionally painful experience makes anyone rude or careless or insufficiently evolved. But the default “I’m sorry” most of us reach for when confronted with breakup news paints the dissolution of a relationship as a universal loss, reinforcing the dated idea that being partnered is paradise and being single is sad.

“There are a lot of societal, cultural, or even personal projections made when we automatically assume someone is devastated after a breakup,” explains therapist Lindsey Brock, founder of the Breakup Therapist. “It’s never helpful to assume what someone is thinking or how they are responding emotionally to any situation.”.

And sometimes, the breakup is actually good news. “It’s natural for people to say ‘I’m sorry’ because they associate breakups with heartache and want to express sympathy,” says Shannon Lundgren, founder of the matchmaking service Shannon's Circle and author of the upcoming book The Love Funnel. “It’s not the most helpful response because it assumes the person is heartbroken, when they may feel relieved or happy about the ending.”.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps more important than whatever heteropatriarchal norms we may or may not be reinforcing when we apologize to someone for their own breakup is the simple fact that “I’m sorry” might not be an appropriate response to a given situation. This default apology ignores the reality that, in many cases, a breakup might be totally neutral, or even something to celebrate.

“Walking away from a relationship may be the most courageous yet difficult thing someone does,” adds Brock. “Meeting them with an ‘I'm sorry’ may undermine that bravery, or even leave someone second-guessing whether they made the right decision.”.

While the end of a relationship certainly may be cause for sympathy—I myself have had my share of emotionally annihilating splits in which condolences were very much in order—it’s not always appropriate or helpful to automatically assume that someone is struggling just because they’ve been through a breakup.

Industry observers note that “Culturally, we are conditioned to assume that when a relationship ends, it’s a negative thing and that it must therefore be an unfortunate event,” notes relationship coach Natalia Juarez, founder of Lovistics. “While expressing sympathy in some situations is appropriate, it’s essential to consider a variety of factors. Each breakup is unique and multi-faceted.” Rather than reaching for a canned response, “it’s far better to actively listen and be mindful,” says Juarez.

Industry observers note that it's also worth remembering that even the person who initiated the breakup might be struggling. “People assume that if you did the breaking up, that you aren't unhappy about it, but that's not always true,” adds Susan Trombetti, matchmaker and CEO of Exclusive Matchmaking.

This, of course, requires a little more effort than offering the standard post-breakup condolences. Below, a few tips from the pros for approaching breakup news more mindfully.

Don’t assume you know how someone is feeling. An easy way to avoid doing this? Just ask! Instead of reaching for an “Oh, I’m so sorry,” Juarez recommends starting out with a simple “How are you feeling about it?”.

Another option? “Do you want to talk about it, or talk about something else?” suggests Lundgren. It's a simple way to let someone decide whether they're in the mood to unpack the breakup or would rather focus on literally anything else.

“As a general rule, it’s most supportive to ask how someone is feeling about a substantial transition. This gives them room to honor their different feelings and experiences without the pressure to fit some social norm or expectation,” indicates Brock. “They may feel terrified yet hopeful, sad and relieved, guilty yet proud, ecstatic and free.”.

It has been revealed that it's also worth recognizing the courage it can take to end a relationship. “Everyone thinks breakups are awful, but that misses how much bravery it takes to make that decision,” notes Vanessa Errecarte, author of Valuable & Visible.

Sometimes the best thing you can give someone going through something significant is space to embrace what may be a wide range of conflicting emotions.

But know that that might look very different from situation to situation. Before expressing sympathy or offering advice, try asking something along the lines of “How can I support you?” notes Brock. “Sometimes people need someone to celebrate with them, distract them from misery, give sound advice, initiative an adventure, or join them in bashing their ex. When in doubt, just listen and never assume.”.

According to recent reports, support doesn't always have to involve a conversation about the breakup, either. “Inviting someone out to lunch or dinner demonstrates you care,” claims Trombetti. “Just sitting with them is very comforting and shows caring and empathy.”.

In a recent development, asking someone what, if anything, they need instead of assuming makes it much easier to provide actually useful support to a friend who might need it. “Communicating openly is so much better than simply saying, ‘If you need me, I’m here,’” explains Juarez. “The fact is, many broken-hearted people don’t reach out because they don’t want to be a burden.”.

Industry observers note that A little self-reflection never hurts. When confronted with the news of someone else’s split, it may be “helpful to assess and challenge your own beliefs about marriage or long-term partnership,” notes Brock. “While it’s totally okay to want a long-term partnership for yourself, others may not share that as a priority. As you support your friend through their breakup, stay mindful that being single isn’t inherently bad or wrong or just a blip on the radar en route to partnership.”.

Recent findings suggest that instead of treating the end of a relationship as a setback, consider acknowledging the strength it can take to walk away from something that isn't working. “Help the person who's going through the breakup see the strength in making a hard decision,” claims Errecarte.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rosalía was recently spotted walking through the Fresh York City streets with a Dana Toder bag over three feet long.
  • It has been revealed that in case there was any doubt, the point of view was the bag.
  • There’s something undoubtedly beautiful about taking an everyday object and making it obscenely huge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rosalía was recently spotted walking through the Fresh York City streets with a Dana Toder bag over three feet long. Paired with her vintage pink satin ballet platform heels from Junko Shimada, the massive, hulking bag from the emerging designer was the kind of shocking jolt of life and newness that typical fashion paparazzi shots lack.

It has been revealed that in case there was any doubt, the point of view was the bag. Supersized bags are ubiquitous right now: Chanel, Acne Studios, and Bottega Veneta all showcased their own versions for fall/winter 2026, but Toder’s took the idea to a newly introduced level with its extreme size and concept. Consider the bags just one of the many examples of supersizing the everyday. Chandelier earrings and oversize necklaces have never been so big at Saint Laurent and Valentino. Elsewhere, labels like Comme des Garçons, Vaquera, and Givenchy amped up their usual voluminous silhouettes even more for spring/summer 2027. Rising designer Beata Rydbacken is also making the biggest hair clips you’ve ever seen in your entire life.

There’s something undoubtedly beautiful about taking an everyday object and making it obscenely huge. It puts a focus on what some may consider the everyday or mundane and makes it sort of beautifully ludicrous. Dana Toder originally designed her “Baggage Bag” for Krähe, a fashion film by Lili Conzen, shot on 16mm, which will be released in spring 2027. Accompanied by exhibitions in London, Paris, Berlin, and Vienna, which will also showcase the bag, the film questions who gets to be seen in fashion and gives older women the leading roles. “When Lili shared the film’s concept with me, it connected really well with how I see clothes and accessories: as things that go through life with us and hold memories and emotions,” Toder tells ELLE. “I see a woman’s relationship with her bag or her garments as something very emotional and complex. The focus on older women felt especially meaningful when thinking about how those relationships develop over a lifetime.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Toder, it’s also a representation of metaphorical and physical baggage. The print featured on the big bag combines analog photographs from the ’80s to today, taken by the designer, director, and actresses in the film, and plays a role in showcasing the shared experience across different women, ages, and times. The bag itself was also made with the help of her 80-year-old leatherworking mentor, Shmulik.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m interested in everything that becomes emotionally attached to a bag: the things it holds, the places it has been with us, and how the material changes over time. It might hold an object that reminds you of someone, or the bag itself might remind you of a certain period in your life,” she claims.

“We carry all of that around too. I’m always carrying so much stuff, and I love the sight of a woman digging through her bag, with things falling out. I honestly think it’s one of the most beautiful sights. You’re looking for your keys and suddenly going through things that hold so many memories. Some might have been there for two years, or tucked away in your wallet for what feels like forever. I find something very emotional in that everyday moment, coming across parts of your life that you carry without really thinking about them.”.

Sources indicate that seeing the familiar through a campy, oversize lens gives one both feelings of nostalgia and whimsy, and that’s perhaps why we’re experiencing so many humungous accessories lately. In the case of Rydbacken, in addition to her giant hair clips, she’s also made supersized wired earbuds, the biggest studded belt to ever exist, and jumbo pins, with many going viral. In fashion’s current game of scale, the bigger the accessory, the more room it leaves for memory, meaning, and a little bit of spectacle.

#20226. There’s Science Behind Why You’re So Obsessed With Your Partner's Smell

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1439 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cosmopolitan ↗ Open Full Page

There’s Science Behind Why You’re So Obsessed With Your Partner's Smell

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love.
  • Recent findings suggest that you know that thing where your partner's T-shirt somehow smells better after they've worn it?
  • If you've ever wondered why you're so attracted to your partner's natural smell, you've probably heard that pheromones are to blame.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Recent findings suggest that you know that thing where your partner's T-shirt somehow smells better after they've worn it? Or when you find yourself nuzzling into their neck during a hug because you genuinely can't get enough of how they smell? It's not necessarily their cologne, shampoo, or laundry detergent you're into, either. Sometimes, it's just them. And apparently, you're really into it.

If you've ever wondered why you're so attracted to your partner's natural smell, you've probably heard that pheromones are to blame. There's this idea that our bodies can somehow sniff out the people we're most compatible with, even before our brains catch up. But the science behind that theory isn't nearly as straightforward as you might think.

“Researchers haven't definitively identified a human sex pheromone that reliably produces sexual attraction in the way we sometimes see in other species,” explains Casey Tanner, a LELO sexpert and certified sex therapist.

That doesn't mean your partner's smell has nothing to do with your feelings for them, though. Our sense of smell is closely connected to memory and emotion, which helps explain why someone's scent can become so comforting (or downright irresistible) once we're attached to them. But does loving the way your partner smells actually mean you're compatible? And should you be concerned if you don't particularly care for their scent? Here's what the science says.

Pheromones are chemical signals released by one member of a species that can trigger specific behavioral or physical responses in another member of the same species. In the animal kingdom, they play a role in everything from attracting mates to marking territory. But when it comes to humans, things get a little less clear.

According to Tanner, while pheromones are well-documented in other animals, their role in human sexual attraction remains unproven. So, there's no solid scientific evidence that your body is sending out some irresistible chemical signal that makes certain people want to jump your bones.

And while pheromones and body odor often get lumped together, they're not actually the same thing. According to Tanner, your natural body odor is essentially your unique scent signature, shaped by everything from genetics and hormones to skin bacteria, diet, and your environment. Unlike pheromones, which are defined by the biological responses they trigger, ordinary body odor doesn't have to produce a specific response to influence how someone feels about you. So, while you might find someone's body odor incredibly attractive, that doesn't mean you're responding to pheromones.

Research suggests that body odor can influence attraction and who we're drawn to, but scientists are still figuring out exactly how much of a role it plays. And just because someone's natural scent appeals to you doesn't mean your bodies have identified each other as a perfect genetic match.

Recent findings suggest that if you've ever found yourself lingering over your partner's pillow after they've left, there's a reason their scent can feel so comforting. And it has a lot to do with how closely our sense of smell is connected to memory and emotion.

It has been revealed that “When we're falling for someone, their smell can become intertwined with experiences of pleasure, affection, comfort, and arousal,” Tanner explains. “Over time, that scent can become a kind of shortcut to feeling close to that person!”.

Basically, your brain starts associating your partner's natural scent with all the things you love about being around them, from cuddling on the couch to having sex. And those associations can stick around even when you're physically apart.

It has been revealed that “Once we’re attached to that person, their body odor essentially becomes a reinforcement or reward,” claims psychologist Pamela Dalton, PhD, MPH. Their scent can bring back positive memories and feelings of intimacy, which helps explain why something as simple as a worn shirt can make you feel closer to someone you're missing.

It has been revealed that as much as we'd love to tell you that being obsessed with your partner's natural scent means you've found your soulmate, science doesn't exactly back that up. Sure, there may be some biological factors at play, but liking the way someone smells isn't proof that you're genetically compatible, much less destined to spend your lives together.

It has been revealed that some research has explored whether people are more attracted to the body odor of potential partners whose immune-system genes differ from their own. The theory is that these differences could lead to greater immune diversity in biological offspring. But according to Tanner, the findings have been inconsistent, and there's no reliable evidence that humans choose romantic partners based on genetic compatibility.

And even if someone's scent makes you want to bury your face in their chest 24/7, that doesn't tell you much about whether you'll actually work as a couple.

Sources indicate that “Loving your partner's scent can be a true reflection of attraction and attachment, but no, it’s not a reliable diagnostic tool for long-term compatibility,” Tanner says. “Chemistry is a great indicator of initial attraction, but compatibility is something we have to discover, negotiate, and create over time.”.

In a recent development, in other words, enjoying someone's natural smell is a nice bonus, but it's not a substitute for shared values, trust, communication, or the other things that make a relationship work. And if you're not immediately drawn to someone's scent, that doesn't mean attraction can't develop as you get to know them.

According to recent reports, if you've made it this far and realized you've never once felt the urge to steal your partner's T-shirt just to smell it, don't stress. Not everyone is particularly sensitive to scent, and being indifferent to your partner's natural smell doesn't mean you're any less attracted to them.

According to recent reports, according to Tanner, people vary in how sensitive they are to smells, how much attention they pay to them, and how notable scent is to their experience of attraction. Some people might be more drawn to their partner's appearance, voice, personality, or the emotional connection they share.

“If you’re indifferent to a person’s smell, it’s likely not going to be a game-changer because once you have the opportunity to get to know the person, you find [other] positives and compatibility between the two of you,” notes Dalton.

It has been revealed that and if you're otherwise happy with your relationship, there's no reason to start questioning it just because your partner's scent doesn't do anything special for you. As Tanner puts it, “If you’re into them, don’t go looking for a problem just because you haven’t noticed their scent!”.

Okay, but what if you used to love your partner's natural scent and now you can't stand it? Before you start questioning your entire relationship, know that a change in how you perceive someone's smell doesn't automatically mean your feelings for them have changed.

Industry observers note that according to Tanner, everything from hormonal fluctuations and medications to diet, illness, and changes in your sense of smell can affect how you experience your partner's scent. Pregnancy, for example, can make you more sensitive to certain smells. And sometimes, the explanation is as simple as your partner switching shampoos or laundry detergents.

Industry observers note that of course, emotions can play a role, too. Because scent is so closely connected to memory and feelings, your associations with someone's smell can change as your relationship evolves.

According to recent reports, “There is evidence that when, for whatever reason, that relationship isn’t working, that body odor is no longer pleasant or preferred,” states Dalton. “All of a sudden, because of the association with negative characteristics, [the body odor] is changing. Your response is changing.”.

Industry observers note that still, suddenly disliking your partner's scent isn't proof that something is wrong between you. As Tanner explains, a change in smell isn't a reliable indicator of relationship conflict, and there may be a physical explanation worth considering first.

According to recent reports, if you notice a significant change in your partner's actual body odor, it's worth gently asking whether anything has changed with their health, medications, or routine. And if there's a particularly noticeable change in genital odor, Tanner recommends encouraging them to check in with a healthcare professional.

Sources indicate that bottom line: A change in how your partner smells to you isn't automatically a sign that something's wrong. How you feel about your partner's scent can change for all sorts of reasons, and it's just one small part of the bigger picture.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that everything smells like vanilla.
  • But hundreds of other fragrance rolls out in 2026 deserve a spot on your vanity and a spritz on your skin, and many are far less sweet.
  • See all the winners of the 2026 Harper’s Bazaar Fragrance Awards, plus quotes from our beauty editors on what makes these formulas worthy of your next blind buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that everything smells like vanilla. At least, that’s what perfume naysayers will tell you. And it’s somewhat true: If you’re judging by what’s popular, ubiquitous, or cool with the youth, then sure—vanilla scents and sweet gourmands are still trending.

But hundreds of other fragrance rolls out in 2026 deserve a spot on your vanity and a spritz on your skin, and many are far less sweet. Gourmands took a turn for the weird and fruity this year, with notes like lychee and rice milk popping up in otherwise innocuous formulas. Woods and ambers continued to reign, as did spice-forward and citrus scents with unexpected depth. Perfumers are meeting our demand for newness in increasingly interesting, artistic ways, and we smelled hundreds of their creations to choose the 63 winners of our annual fragrance awards.

See all the winners of the 2026 Harper’s Bazaar Fragrance Awards, plus quotes from our beauty editors on what makes these formulas worthy of your next blind buy.

Chanel Coco Mademoiselle Crush Absolu.

Industry observers note that “Perfumer Olivier Polge reinvented the beloved “Coco Mad” scent as Crush Absolu, a new juice centered around patchouli, amber, rose, and a lychee-grapefruit accord. ‘There’s something voluptuous, something very prideful, something very addictive,’ Polge states about the new scent.”.

In a recent development, “The new iteration of J’adore was inspired by Rihanna herself. As such, it’s a sweeter, bolder take, with notes of honeyed jasmine, rose, ylang-ylang, and vanilla.” —JR.

Guerlain L'Heure Bleue Eau de Parfum.

"Bazaar’s Beauty Commerce Editor, Tiffany Dodson Davis, describes Guerlain’s L’Heure Bleue Eau de Parfum as the “scent of sunset,” thanks to a blue-sky accord that evokes the moment the sun goes down and the air turns crisp, clean, and fresh." —KI.

Burberry Goddess Amber Vanilla Eau de Parfum Intense.

It has been revealed that “Lavender, maple syrup, four vanilla notes—I feel like a dog hearing all my favorite words. The result is a warm, ambery gourmand perfume that’s perfect for the cooler months.” —JR.

Armani Beauty Emporio Armani Power of You Eau de Parfum.

Recent findings suggest that "Passionfruit adds an unexpected zing to the vanilla base here, making Power of You one of our favorite tropical-leaning gourmands of the year. It's pure summertime sex appeal." —JR.

“Henry Rose Ripe captures fruits—from lychee to watermelon—at their juiciest, ripest point, like a delectable first bite, before packing a punch with black pepper, cardamom, and powdery florals.” —Katie Intner, beauty market and commerce editor.

Influxious Magic Hour Eau de Parfum.

“One of the most unexpected fruity florals on the list, Influxious Magic Hour melds watermelon and dragon fruit with spicy chili pepper for a burst of juicy energy.” —KI.

Balmain Paris Destin De Balmain Eau de Parfum.

Sources indicate that "The opening note of Destin is strawberry, a modern and sweet fruity note that quickly dries down to a patchouli-forward, gorgeous floral musk. It will make you smell expensive." —JR.

In a recent development, "Neroli, bergamot, and yuzu combine with notes of orange blossom, jasmine, and tonka bean for a well-rounded fragrance that stands out from the pack. Parfum de Marly's Athénaïs eau de parfum has a zesty composition upon first spritz before drying down to a powdery finish." —Tiffany Dodson Davis, beauty commerce editor.

Industry observers note that “Gap recently brought back its iconic fragrance line from the ’90s, including the nostalgic Grass Eau de Parfum. It now features matcha, vetiver, green mandarin, and cedar for a fresh take on its outdoorsy, earthy scent.” —KI.

Maison Francis Kurkdjian Oud Velvet Mood Extrait de Parfum.

“For those who are oud-averse, Maison Francis Kurkdjian’s Oud Velvet Mood is a lighter iteration of the category. The oud has a woody quality, and when paired with spicy cinnamon, rich saffron, and juicy peach, the result is light and warm like the sun.” —KI.

“This stunning perfume is all gardenia and vanilla, and in its simplicity, it happens to be one of our most complimented scents of the year.” —JR.

Balenciaga Pink Oud Extrait de Parfum.

Sources indicate that "This is a bold, long-wearing scent for those who live and die for the sensual pairing of rose and oud. We're obsessed with the way it blooms and evolves on skin throughout the night." —JR.

Ex Nihilo Demon Dancer Eau de Parfum.

“Ex Nihilo Demon Dancer feels like moving through the crisp air on a spring day, with peppermint providing a breezy contrast to juicy rhubarb, bright bergamot, and warm tonka bean.” —KI.

“We don’t know what we love more: the magnetic floral perfume that begs to be worn every day, the sculptural bottle, or the bookish packaging that made us a fan before we even took our first whiff.” —JR.

“You can’t go wrong with Beyoncé’s sultry and sophisticated hair perfume, which leaves hair with a long-wearing trail of bergamot, jasmine, oud, sandalwood, and Haitian vetiver.” —JR.

Creed Iris Debonair Eau de Parfum.

“Delightfully unisex, this aromatic scent is a masterclass in balance. The top opens with bergamot, cardamom, pink pepper, and wormwood. In the middle, you’ll find fruity fig, lavender, and violet leaf. The base is iris, amberwood, and ambrette.” —JR.

D.S. & Durga Resurrected Corpse Flower.

“Earthy and green, with an olive top note and banana base note—this is the perfume to buy this year if you want to smell wholly original and unabashedly cool.” —JR.

In a recent development, “Creamy and warm with notes of chocolate and coffee, this is the must-have gourmand perfume of the winter. In a word, it makes us feel happy.” —JR.

Discothèque Next to Me or Nothing Eau De Parfum.

“More of a feeling than a fragrance, this scent is airy and easy to wear, with breezy notes of milk, jasmine, and woods.” —JR.

Phlur Heavy Cream Eau de Parfum.

"Gourmand lovers will want to overindulge in this elevated eau de parfum, which combines two types of creams—whipped and coconut—along with jasmine blossom and vanilla mousse notes for a sophisticated yet playful olfactory blend." —TDD.

“An olfactory version of a sound bath, Liis Forest Sounds boasts notes of bright yuzu, damp rain (earthier than plain water), green leaves, and woods.” —KI.

Dolce&Gabbana Dolce&Gabbana Your Devotion Eau de Parfum Intense.

Industry observers note that "The notes in this fragrance sound good enough to eat: Sicilian lemon, orange blossom, and vanilla milk. This is a date-night, delicious gourmand for those who usually prefer a lighter citrus scent." —JR.

Dries Van Noten Velvet Violet Eau de Parfum.

“This woody-gourmand scent captures the lush texture of velvet with a mix of unusual notes: violet leaf, clary sage essence, toasted sesame, barley roasted, and grilled tonka beans.” —JR.

Ellis Brooklyn Vanilla Rice Eau de Parfum.

It has been revealed that “Rather than wrapping yourself in a cashmere blanket on a cold day, try wearing Ellis Brooklyn’s Vanilla Rice. It combines the warm notes of toasted rice, cherry blossom, sweet vanilla, and creamy coconut milk for a soft, slightly floral scent.” —KI.

Estée Lauder Glimmer Eau de Parfum Spray.

“Estée Lauder’s Glimmer gives crisp orange flower and rose a warm finish with vanilla bean, tonka bean, amber, and two types of wood.” —KI.

Glossier You Soie Eau de Parfum.

“The latest addition to Glossier’s You fragrance lineup, Soie is an aquatic and solar take on a floral scent, with tropical Tiare flower water and creamy rice in place of powdery florals.” —KI.

“Not quite a fragrance, Future Society’s Base Scent is like the no-makeup makeup version of perfume. Infused with prebiotics and a patent-pending technology, the scent is designed to enhance and balance any fragrance layered beneath it—whether that’s lotion, deodorant, or your natural scent—by working with the skin’s microbiome.” —KI.

Harlem Perfume Co. Sensual Muse Eau de Parfum.

“A fruity floral that reads as more sophisticated, Harlem Fragrance Co.’s Sensual Muse gives juicy apricot, bright citrus, and creamy gardenia a warm, compelling character once whipped vanilla, sandalwood, and amber are added into the mix.” —KI.

“If you prefer your cocktails in fragrance form, look no further than By Kilian, which has mastered the art of turning a nutty, warm, slightly sweet espresso martini into a wearable scent that feels especially seductive at night.” —KI.

How Were the 2026 Fragrance Award Winners Chosen?

Our editors test more than 1,000 fresh introduces every year to identify the most innovative releases across every beauty category. The Bazaar Fragrance Awards winners represent the perfumes we fell in love with this year during our extensive testing. For the 2026 Fragrance Awards, Bazaar enlisted fragrance experts and perfume superfans (ourselves included) to curate a list of bottles that deserve a spot on your vanity.

For more than 150 years, Harper’s Bazaar has been the preeminent fashion and beauty resource for women at every age. We cover what’s new and what’s next in beauty by working with the world’s leading authorities in dermatology, plastic surgery, cosmetics, skincare, haircare, and fragrance. Every story we publish has been thoroughly researched and vetted by our team of beauty editors and industry experts.

#20212. Has Zegna Cracked the Code to Modern Tailoring?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (786 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

Has Zegna Cracked the Code to Modern Tailoring?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pay attention to the world of menswear long enough, and you’ll notice that certain quandaries come up time and again.
  • According to Alessandro Sartori, the artistic director of Zegna for a little more than a decade now, there’s another question we should all be asking ourselves: What exactly is a suit these days?
  • “Everything we do here is grounded in tailoring techniques and in tailoring fabrics,” Sartori tells me over Zoom from his home in Milan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pay attention to the world of menswear long enough, and you’ll notice that certain quandaries come up time and again. A favorite among traditionalists and avant-garde types alike is the fate of the suit. It’s been incorrectly declared dead enough times that the handwringing over its demise has largely shifted to questions of its evolving role in the modern guy’s wardrobe: Who wears a suit, and when, and why?

According to Alessandro Sartori, the artistic director of Zegna for a little more than a decade now, there’s another question we should all be asking ourselves: What exactly is a suit these days?

“Everything we do here is grounded in tailoring techniques and in tailoring fabrics,” Sartori tells me over Zoom from his home in Milan. “But I'm a massive believer that a suit doesn't necessarily have to be a combination of the classic top and the classic bottom in the same fabric and color.” It can be comprised of those things, he stresses. But the “modern suit,” as he calls it, can also be an intentional pairing of a different kind of top—a chore coat, an overshirt—with a trouser with a different fabrication. The materials and colors should feel complementary and cohesive but needn’t be perfectly matched.

“This is not only a way to give a upcoming life to suiting,” he explains, “but to dress men differently—and, at the same time, keep the quality, the craft, and the beautiful fit that a tailored piece has.”.

According to recent reports, the idea is to adapt classic techniques to the realities of getting dressed today. “Many fashion brands offer a nice quality, but is not the handmade quality that we do,” Sartori indicates. “And there are a lot of brands that are offering beautiful, beautiful quality, but they are quite classic.” Since he started in 2016, Sartori’s overarching project has been to populate the gulf between those two modes of production, making clothes that feel contemporary but are rooted in the top-tier fabrics and handwork that helped Zegna become the powerhouse of Italian fashion that it is today.

It has been revealed that the latest addition to Sartori’s lineup is a latest jacket, the Falcon. It pays homage to the sort of utilitarian jackets Zegna founder Ermenegildo Zegna might have worn while walking the grounds of what is now the Oasi Zegna nature reserve in northern Italy, at the base of the Biellese Alps. (According to firm lore, Ermenegildo imagined those walks as being accompanied by the flight of a falcon.).

In a recent development, sartori acknowledges that the use case, in 2026, might be a little different. “I don't think that people are necessarily using the jacket walking up in the mountains,” he states. The Falcon is more about embracing a “sporty-chic attitude,” whether you’re stomping around the country or the city, and working within the modular framework that the designer has created at Zegna. You can mix and match it with other pieces—both old and fresh—from the brand, and you can wear it as part of a “modern suit” or on its own.

In a recent development, the upcoming design is cut from Zegna’s Oasi Cashmere for lightweight warmth, and Sartori calls it “a great addition to our vocabulary.” Buttoned patch pockets give you somewhere to stash your stuff, a bowling collar can be flipped up to shield against stiff winds, and an internal drawstring can be cinched at the midsection for a little extra protection against the cold. Ultimately, it’s a familiar-looking piece. But it’s exceptional in its construction and materials and its design—a streamlined take on the hunting jackets of yore—is as considered as how it’s made.

In a recent development, “Long-lasting life is a key factor for what we're doing, and I don't mean only quality-wise,” Sartori claims. “I also mean design-wise.”.

According to recent reports, the designer, for his part, hopes that the Falcon—alongside other modern classics from the brand—will be the sort of thing that guys wear and reinterpret for years before passing it on to the next generation. And as the brand continues to grow and evolve alongside its customer base, one of his biggest aims is to ensure that each item he introduces remains relevant throughout its (ideally long) lifespan.

Industry observers note that “It’s like writing a book, and every season I add a chapter,” he claims. “Because the story is going on, is moving with our clients, our community of people, our brand, our family. So many layers are … I don’t want to say ready, but cooking. I see a bright future for the brand, following this principle of walking with our customers and building an indelible aesthetic. I like this approach.”.

#20186. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Latest York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1262 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Latest York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit.
  • It has been revealed that as a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood.
  • Recent findings suggest that in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

It has been revealed that as a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a latest lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

Recent findings suggest that in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in Newly introduced York City.

According to recent reports, it felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a newly introduced role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

Sources indicate that for me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

According to recent reports, “How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

Sources indicate that I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Upcoming York.

In the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

According to recent reports, the table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

Sources indicate that at the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

It has been revealed that as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in Newly introduced York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.
