Breaking: The Horse Girl Trend Is Here for Your Jewelry Box

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • In a recent development, saddles, stirrups, and horseshoes, oh my: We’ve been firmly in the year of the Fire Horse since February 2026, and the jewelry scene is officially in its horse girl era.
  • Celebrities are clearly fans: Taylor Swift just wore two double-layered horseshoe pendants to announce her Grammy nomination.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In a recent development, saddles, stirrups, and horseshoes, oh my: We’ve been firmly in the year of the Fire Horse since February 2026, and the jewelry scene is officially in its horse girl era. Aside from the look being a clear classic in the world of jewelry (horseshoes were popular in Victorian-era jewels), today’s examples vary from sparkly creations to more minimal, toned-down pieces with everyday appeal. No matter the aesthetic, the jewelry of the Year of the Fire Horse is strong: This era only comes around every 60 years in the Chinese zodiac and is said to represent strength, independence, and fearlessness.

Celebrities are clearly fans: Taylor Swift just wore two double-layered horseshoe pendants to announce her Grammy nomination. Horse-ified jewelry also spanned the runway. For spring/summer 2027, both Gucci and Celine revisited the archival horsebit hardware detail and reworked it in a contemporary way to highlight the beautiful lines and sculptural symmetry of the timeless motif. Elsewhere, Chloé’s statement belt covered in huge running horses has been a fashion girl favorite and is the equivalent of jewelry for your waist.

Industry observers note that there is perhaps nothing more classic than a chunky horseshoe ring or a horse-themed charm. Verragio and Oscar Heyman each reworked the symbol in gemstone-studded bracelets and double-motif rings. Elsewhere, Lionheart makes a slew of gloriously stunning oversize horse-head pendants and brooches brimming with diamonds and, sometimes, accessorized with mother-of-pearl saddles. The brand also partners directly with 13 Hands Equine Rescue, a nonprofit sanctuary located in Clinton Corners, Newly introduced York.

But this year, equestrian jewelry is not horsing around when it comes to experimenting. One such example is Hermès’s latest collection, which has an obvious horse connection: saddles, diamond-decked horse heads, and golden saddles. Titled “Into the Horsescape,” the 90-piece lineup is quite literally the horse girl’s dream: lassos in the form of massive baguette-cut diamonds and glimmering oversize horsebit bracelets replete with pavé brown and white diamonds. Pomellato also showcased a carved horse cameo surrounded by brown diamonds and suspended from a delicate rose-gold Dressage-link chain.

If you want to lean into your inner horse girl in a more subtle, everyday way, Gucci’s iconic horsebit rings, refined drop earrings, and sleek bangles offer a sophisticated and versatile place to start your collection. Going vintage is another option: Equestrian themes have been reinterpreted in the jewelry space for hundreds of years now, so there’s ample opportunity. One thing is clear: Horse girl jewelry is galloping from the archives to the runway and into everyday style.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that while she delights in sharing the stage with her husband, Rinna also enjoys the solitude of her backstage getting-ready routine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some couples wouldn’t dare mix love and work, but Lisa Rinna and Harry Hamlin beg to differ. “I love working with Harry because he’s professional, hardworking, and he knows his lines,” Rinna tells Vogue. “But the best part of working with him is that I get to sleep with him, and it doesn’t cause a scandal!”.

Last night, Rinna and Hamlin celebrated the opening night of It’s A Wonderful Life: A Live Radio Play on Broadway (she’s Violet; he’s Mr. Potter), joining Broadway legends Andrew Rannells, Megan Hilty, and Tituss Burgess on the call sheet. “Our family watches It’s A Wonderful Life every year on Christmas Eve. We love the movie so much, so when we got the call that Broadway legend Jerry Zaks was directing, it was a no-brainer,” Rinna says. “The first thing I asked Jerry when he cast us was: Who thought to put Broadway icons in a cast with Lisa Rinna and Harry Hamlin? He didn’t really have an answer, but he likes us all together.”.

Recent findings suggest that while she delights in sharing the stage with her husband, Rinna also enjoys the solitude of her backstage getting-ready routine. “I am someone who loves to have music playing, and I am a bit superstitious, so I have specific songs that I have to listen to before each show,” she claims. On the It’s A Wonderful Life playlist? “While I am getting my wig put on, I listen to the La Bola Negra soundtrack. Then we go to Whitney Houston’s Greatest Hits—we listen to ‘Heartbreak Hotel’ and ‘It’s Not Right, But It’s Okay.’ Finally, right before the five-minute call, I listen to ‘Party’ by Troye Sivan.”.

Sources indicate that rinna wanted to convey the holiday spirit through her premiere night look. “I had a vision of myself wearing a Willy Chavarria men’s suit,” she states. “[My stylist, Daniela Romero] found this one for me, and I’m absolutely in love with the color. She took my vision and added a nod to the holidays. I am a cunty Grinch, how perfect!” For the after-party, Rinna opted for a look from her longtime friend Sergio Hudson. “I wanted to wear American designers for opening night,” she says. “I am excited to have a piece of [Sergio] with me tonight.”.

Here, Lisa Rinna brings Vogue along for the opening night of It’s A Wonderful Life: A Live Radio Play on Broadway.

Getting ready for the carpet with my incredible hair and makeup team—Jae Cardenas and Katie Nova.

My love. 20 years later, and we’re back on Broadway together… Harry and I played Roxie Hart and Billy Flynn in Chicago in 2007, returning to Broadway together has been the most full-circle dream come true!

It is certainly a wonderful life.

Harry and I really have been loving this chapter together in Newly introduced York…dare I say it suits us?!

The inspiration for this look—cunty Grinch holiday realness.

Beep beep bitches, we’re on Broadway!!!

Catch us at the Broadhurst through January 3rd.

1945 called and you better believe I answered.

This show, these people bring us so much joy.

In addition to Lana Sherwood, I get to voice Violet, Zuzu, and a few other characters. Such a treat.

The icon Andrew Rannalls—our most perfect George Bailey!

After party look by Sergio Hudson.

It has been revealed that still pinching myself, truly. This entire experience has been such a dream, I’m so grateful.

#20172. Tech Report: Silver Eye Makeup: “Stardust” Makeup Is Here to Bring Whimsy to Your Holiday Glam

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1083 w)

Tech Report: Silver Eye Makeup: “Stardust” Makeup Is Here to Bring Whimsy to Your Holiday Glam

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that no matter your feelings on how festive is too festive during the holiday season (for the record, we’re pro decorating your home like a European Christmas market from November to February), there’s one universal rule when it comes to beauty looks during this time that we can all agree on: The holidays were meant for glitter.
  • Industry observers note that this is more than just putting on a glitter eyeshadow or some tinsel in your hair.
  • “[It]’s something magical that gives us the same feeling we had as kids opening presents,” adds celebrity makeup artist Alexandra French.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that no matter your feelings on how festive is too festive during the holiday season (for the record, we’re pro decorating your home like a European Christmas market from November to February), there’s one universal rule when it comes to beauty looks during this time that we can all agree on: The holidays were meant for glitter. And this year, we’re leaning into a more whimsical take on looking all shiny and bright. Say hello to “stardust” makeup.

Industry observers note that this is more than just putting on a glitter eyeshadow or some tinsel in your hair. “Stardust” evokes a warm, nostalgic feeling and sprinkles some magic along the way. “Adding a pop of shimmer is such an act of self-celebration, and it feels really good,” indicates Donni Davy, celebrity makeup artist and founder of Half Magic. “It’s like decorating your face the same way you buy something beautiful for your home. It’s a feel-good thing that also sparks conversation and joy in other people and inspires other people to do the same.”.

“[It]’s something magical that gives us the same feeling we had as kids opening presents,” adds celebrity makeup artist Alexandra French. “I’m always letting my inner child play when creating these looks. I’ll never not be whimsical.".

Recent findings suggest that the most obvious way to add some sparkle is with the eyes. But for that “stardust” effect, there’s a delicate art to it. “Stardust eyes are all about creating that dreamy, ethereal twinkling effect,” notes Davy. “It's not about packing on a ton of glitter; it’s more about these delicate flashes of sparkle that catch in the light in a really magical way.”.

The key to the “stardust” effect is in the application. Compared to traditional glitter or gems, Davy says that stardust eyes are more subtle. “It’s almost like a dusting that catches the light in a totally unexpected and very flattering way.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Davy, she loves starting with a soft wash of color (pale pink, lavender, or champagne are her personal picks) on the lids, like Half Magic’s Duo-Chrome Eyeshadow in Blushing Lizard. You can also try Saie’s viral Supersuede Baked Eyeshadow in Bellini or K-beauty’s Hince Chill Wave for the same shimmer effect. Apply shadow with your fingers, she instructs, focusing on the center of the lid and then blending out. “You want the sparkle to look almost random, rather than perfectly placed,” she notes. “If you want a bit of a grungier look, you can use a brush to apply some underneath your eye as well.”.

For a more ethereal look, build up the shine. She recommends adding some color to the inner and outer waterline corners for added dimension and again all over your eyelids. “You’re going to feel like yourself, but just sparkly,” Davy states.

Sources indicate that but for those who want to go full glam, pack it all on. Think Alix Earle’s Halloween costume as a “gynoid.” Inspired by Japanese illustrator and artist Hajime Sorayama’s “sexy robot” illustrations, French leaned all the way in with silver.

It has been revealed that “I always noted for silver eye makeup to look truly metallic you need to layer different levels of textures and finish it off with a high-shine sparkle,” French claims. “I wanted the eyes to feel like this mask that sparkles and looks alive the way his paintings feel so alive. I wanted people to stop in their tracks when they saw it from across the room.”.

Here, she layered the Urban Decay Chrome Melt Eye Shadow in Temper Tantrum on top of the MAC Dazzleshadow Liquid Eyeshadow for that bold metallic eye. Then she topped it off with Question Beauty Silver Mirror Glitter (her pro tip: Use eyelash glue for application with this) to elevate the metallic look and get something with a more reflective sheen.

But no matter how intense you go with your eye look, both Davy and French say you can never go wrong with sparkle. “It’s a simple way to add a little something to your everyday makeup,” says French.

Why stop at just the eyes? This holiday season, experts say to sprinkle some “stardust” all over. For the body, Davy likes shimmer on the collarbones, shoulders, and décolletage. “Especially if you’re wearing something that indicates a little skin,” she states. Try Half Magic’s Glitterpuck, which she says is a water-based formula made for zero glitter fallout, or we love the Marc Jacobs Money Shot Highlighter and Eva NYC’s Lightweight Silver Hair & Body Glitter Shimmer Spray for an iridescent shine. French recommends using the One/Size On ’Til Dawn Mattifying Waterproof Setting Spray mixed with glitter. She also recommends using the Fenty Beauty Diamond Bomb All-Over Diamond Veil for some body sparkle and more. “It’s the best,” she says. “I use it in the hair as well.”.

It has been revealed that and everyone’s nails have been getting the stardust treatment as early as October, with Taylor Swift wearing a faint, gold “fairy dust”shimmer on her nails at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala. If shadow or body glitter doesn’t speak to you, stardust nails might be the perfect fit.

Sources indicate that “I love depth and dimension, and that’s exactly what this is,” says celebrity nail artist Tom Bachik. “The way this differs from just applying a cat eye or a chrome powder is by actually adding them all. It’s all about layering to get that Stardust effect. You want to have a nice shimmer and iridescence, and chunky glitter, and even a few rhinestones thrown in for good measure.”.

Inspired by Christmas, Bachik wanted to play off gold with a pink iridescent shimmer for Selena Gomez’s latest mani. It’s a subtle pop of color that gives that golden sparkle some added depth. He used the Apreś Nails Maisie Neutral Coffin Gelx Tips before painting on BS-101 and Cosmic Chrome in Etherea from his own collection. Then he used a 3-D gel for that raised gold detail for a nice added touch, and to capture all that holiday spirit. “People love a little sparkle and this is the time of year that actually gives you permission to wear it,” he states.

Industry observers note that so go get your whimsy on this holiday season. It’ll make this time just a little bit more special.

One Martini to Rule Them All

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At a dinner a few years ago, my fiancé’s mother, an elegant former Wall Street banker, ordered a vodka martini, dry, with three olives.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’m not the only one.
  • For those that insist that a true martini must only be made with gin, Tristan Stephenson, host of The Curious Bartender podcast, says, “History isn’t on the side of purists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a dinner a few years ago, my fiancé’s mother, an elegant former Wall Street banker, ordered a vodka martini, dry, with three olives. I grew up in New Orleans, where I was weaned on sickeningly sweet, sticky cocktails, but I was always fascinated by the martini’s sophistication. I’d seen the drink in the hands of characters like Roger Sterling from Mad Men, who would expertly balance his V-shaped glass as he dropped a cynical witticism. So that night, I told the waiter to make it two. Ever since then, I have favored vodka martinis over gin, the base spirit for the by-the-books recipe.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not the only one. Bartenders in Upcoming York have started to notice a trend away from gin. Chris Amirault of Bar Chimera in Manhattan notes that he makes four vodka martinis for every one gin martini. “Vodka pays the bills, and it’s what a lot of people prefer,” says Brian Evans of the Lobby Bar at the Hotel Chelsea, also in Manhattan.

For those that insist that a true martini must only be made with gin, Tristan Stephenson, host of The Curious Bartender podcast, says, “History isn’t on the side of purists. The martini has been a moving target since the 1880s. It started sweeter, with maraschino, orange curaçao, and sugar syrup making appearances. Then it dried out over decades, then had the vermouth all but exorcised from it. Then came olive brine and everything since.”.

Recent findings suggest that why do many martini drinkers prefer vodka? Ti Adelaide Martin, coproprietor of New Orleans staple Commander’s Palace, succinctly explains one reason: “Vodka is the more approachable spirit.” Unlike gin, whose botanicals impart noticeable flavors to a martini, vodka doesn’t overpower other ingredients. It’s more of a blank canvas, which is why it’s used for variations like the espresso martini, which is now the fifth-most-ordered drink at bars, according to Drinks International. Instead of strong flavor, vodka provides “texture, weight, and a kind of icy austerity that can be genuinely beautiful when the vodka is good and the drink is properly cold,” claims Stephenson.

And, let’s be honest, we also drink vodka martinis for the booze. “Vodka tastes bracing,” says Esquire editor-in-chief Michael Sebastian. “I want to take a sip of my martini and get the feeling that it’s strong and it's cold, and it goes through your whole body and you feel better and loose immediately.”.

In a recent development, now I order my vodka martini with a splash of vermouth, just dirty enough to make me thirsty, and shaken so that thin ice shards float on top. You might prefer yours vermouth forward, citrus focused, or dirty as swamp water. It’s all fair game. And that’s the beauty of a vodka martini: It’s a personal drink. My future mother-in-law has her order, and I have mine. What’s yours going to be?

#20145. Latest Update: Lafayette 148’s Emily Smith on 30 Years in Fashion and Finding Her Uniform

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1758 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Lafayette 148’s Emily Smith on 30 Years in Fashion and Finding Her Uniform

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between.
  • I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher.
  • At a certain point, I discovered Donna Karan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Lafayette 148 creative director Emily Smith as the Upcoming York-based fashion house celebrates its 30th anniversary. Smith has spent more than two decades at the helm of the brand, working her way up from a part-time freelancer to creative lead. But her fashion ambitions began long before she arrived in New York. Growing up in Atlanta, she ran her own neighborhood art camp before discovering designers like Donna Karan and realizing fashion could be a career. Now, Smith is celebrating the women who have shaped Lafayette 148 through its “Uniform” campaign, which highlights accomplished New Yorkers and their individual approaches to personal style. Below, Smith reflects on her unconventional start, why she’s stayed at the manufacturer for over 20 years, and the career advice she wishes she’d followed sooner.

I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher. It was basically babysitting all the neighborhood kids, but I created a flyer, got paid for it, and did the whole thing. I started in second grade, and we did it every year for about eight years. I even started hiring people so we could have two classes going at once. We had swimming lessons. The local news even came and did a segment on it. I loved decorating my classroom and setting everything up. My parents were so nice to give me the garage and basement to do it all. Not necessarily an official job, but my first money-making moment.

I was a bagger at Kroger. It just was not for me.

I was always creative growing up. At a certain point, I discovered Donna Karan. It’s kind of crazy when you see somebody doing something and suddenly realize, Oh, that’s a career. I can do that. I became obsessed with everything in the ’90s, all the Newly introduced York fashion at the time. That was when I decided I wanted to pursue it. When college applications came around, my mom really encouraged me to go to art school. I started in fashion, and that became my focus. Growing up in Atlanta, I wasn’t necessarily surrounded by a massive fashion community. But my dad’s office was across the street from the art museum at one point, and I remember going there and having that exposure. My mom was always crafty and creative, too. She really encouraged us to be who we were.

It has been revealed that there’s a language creative people have that’s a little different from the way business people communicate. When I went to art school, I felt like I’d found my people. It wasn’t just fashion people. It was photographers, fine artists, and all these different kinds of creatives. Being around people who thought about things differently was really inspiring. Even today, I thrive around people who have creative insight. There’s always a little more depth to the way they see things.

I interned at Bill Blass for about six months. I moved to Upcoming York in July 2001, and we had our fashion show on September 10. I remember Marc Jacobs had his show that day, too, and everybody was celebrating. People were saying, “Just come a little late to work tomorrow.” And then, obviously, September 11 happened. A week later, the entire team was let go, from the top down. What I learned from that experience was the fragility of everything. Don’t take anything for granted. Anything can come and go in a moment. But I also worked with Lars Nilsson and Hervé Pierre Braillard, who were just the kindest people. This industry has a little bit of everything, but I loved that they led with kindness, even when they were under so much pressure. As an intern, I was literally carrying ironing boards down the street and doing a sketch here or there. It was very much about doing whatever needed to be done.

Sources indicate that after my internship, I had a brief stint of freelancing. Those were some long months. I remember coming home from one job and my roommates asking how my day was. I noted, “Well, I was putting pigs on socks.” I knew I wouldn’t be going back. Freelancing is hard. It’s a grind, but you meet a lot of great people. I actually made some really good contacts during that time. I eventually met Deirdre [Quinn], Lafayette 148’s founder. She met with me on a Saturday, which I thought was incredible. I was really just looking for advice. I wasn’t looking for a job, and I didn’t even know much about the brand. It was only five years old. She was so kind, full of knowledge, and passionate. After I spent a year freelancing and meeting people who seemed so over the industry, her enthusiasm reminded me why I wanted to do this in the first place. She offered me a part-time freelance position, and the rest is history.

In the beginning, security was really notable to me. The idea of losing a job and having to pay rent was scary, so that was definitely part of it initially. But really, it was the growth. Within a couple of years, they were sending me to the factory. It was a small, tight-knit firm, so I was able to wear a lot of different hats. I had a mentor named Barbara Gast who was traveling back and forth from Italy, and I was learning so much from her. I’d compare notes with friends in the industry and realize how much hands-on experience I was getting. I understood the value of that and really loved being so close to the product. It never got boring. And whenever things did get slightly boring, I’d ask, “Okay, what’s next?” And there was always something. It’s such an entrepreneurial place that you can almost create your next opportunity. That’s what made it so exciting.

Recent findings suggest that I think if you asked Deirdre, she’d have a different answer because she has her own experience of building the manufacturer. For me, it’s about having started at a company that was really a factory and being part of the journey of building its identity and what it stands for. I was the kid running up and down the factory floors collecting samples. That hustle and bustle was so innate to who the brand was. To me, it was really exciting to build more of a brand story around that. Thirty years later, we’re still celebrating those roots and making sure we haven’t strayed too far from them, while continuing to evolve. Being part of that journey has been really exciting.

The constant has always been this idea of an accomplished woman. She’s always been at the forefront of who we’re designing for. At the time, it was the career woman. But now, what does that even mean anymore? What does that look like? There are so many different versions of that woman and so many different ways people dress. At the heart of it, she’s a woman who knows what she wants. She’s busy and has a really full life, whether she’s starting her career or ending it. They can all find something in the clothes.

Recent findings suggest that for us, it was about choosing people who inspire us. Number one, they had to be Latest York women. That was the base. We wanted women who make us want to be better ourselves. From someone like Deborah Berke, the architect, to women who have built incredible careers in other fields, it’s vital to shine a light on them. I think back to when I was a kid and how much you need that kind of inspiration. Even at a certain stage in your career, when you’re wondering what the point is, it’s nice to have people who inspire you. These are women who have really built something for themselves, and I think that’s worth celebrating.

In a recent development, sophie de Rakoff said something during the project that I really liked, and I’m going to steal it: “Dressing with intention.” When you know yourself, you know what works on you. It’s no longer about dressing to impress. There’s a confidence in knowing what works for you and making it work. We’re all so busy. Who has time to overthink getting dressed? You know what works, and you build a system around that. You’re able to create a wardrobe that really works for you. Everybody has a different definition of a uniform, and that was the whole point of the project.

When I first started in the industry, I was a total hippie. I was making my own clothes, and they were terrible. Absolutely falling apart. It was what it was. I think part of the change comes from not having as much time as you did when you were younger. But it’s also about simplicity and comfort. I know that if I’m going to be on the floor pinning something but also have to give a presentation, there are certain pieces that work for both. I can be comfortable and still feel appropriately dressed. I’ve found a handful of things that work for me, and I don’t have to think too much about them anymore. A crisp, oversize white cotton button-down is half my closet. I also love a soft skirt and a big chunky sweater. Those are the pieces I always go back to and interchange depending on the day. I even wear sweaters in the summer. It’s cold in the Navy Yard!

Recent findings suggest that our pants fit incredibly well. The moment somebody gets into our pants, they’ll love us forever. Then it’s the jacket and the white shirt. Those three things are our gateway pieces, and everything else follows. You need a good blazer and a good leather piece, too. Once you find those foundational pieces that really work for you, everything else becomes easier.

Sources indicate that I really want to see more women in our clothes. It’s not just about growing the business. It makes me happy when I see people put on our clothes and feel really good. We work so hard to make sure things fit the way a woman wants them to fit. I just want more people to enjoy that.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#20142. Industry News: A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1878 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
  • On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
  • Industry observers note that bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she remarked. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a substantial bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

Industry observers note that bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur remarked. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

Recent findings suggest that over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “Latest Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

It has been revealed that the Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Recent findings suggest that venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary newly introduced guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

Chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in Newly introduced York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

“You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

In 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

In a recent development, you’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

It has been revealed that hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

It has been revealed that be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

Industry observers note that we found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

In a recent development, across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

Industry observers note that at Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

The Colmado, Bur says, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, major sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

It has been revealed that one couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter mentioned, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

James Bond’s Favorite Luggage Brand Has Broken Its Own Rules

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (212 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • James Bond has always travelled in style.
  • Now the company has done something completely left-field.
  • The upcoming GT897 is Globe-Trotter's lightest case yet, and a significant departure from the design that made the brand famous.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Bond has always travelled in style. And while Daniel Craig's 007 was most immediately associated with his Aston Martins, Omega watches, and Tom Ford suits, his luggage of choice was Globe-Trotter, the Hertfordshire-based manufacturer whose cases have also found favor with everyone from Queen Elizabeth II to Kate Moss.

Now the company has done something completely left-field. After 129 years of making essentially the same kind of suitcase, it has changed the formula.

The upcoming GT897 is Globe-Trotter's lightest case yet, and a significant departure from the design that made the brand famous. Out go the traditional rigid frame and locks, replaced by a zip-around opening and softer, more streamlined silhouette.

That said, some familiar details keep it firmly on-brand: the vulcanized fiberboard, leather trim, nickel hardware, and those trademark exposed rivets. And the cases are still handcrafted in Hertfordshire.

According to recent reports, presently available in two color combinations—bland-and-black and green-and-brown—the GT897 is priced at $1,395. A black-and-oxblood version follows in February.

It's an interesting move for a tech giant whose USP has always rested somewhat on its refusal to change. Whether the new James Bond will follow Craig's lead remains to be seen. But at least there's now a new option for packing his tuxedo.

Sources indicate that A minimalist approach to holiday makeup requires multitasking formulas that cover multiple steps without a dozen different products. Look for all-in-one face and eye palettes packed with complementary colors, so you can get party ready without overthinking what goes with what.

Meet your newly introduced getting-ready shortcut: Morphe Sky's the Limit Face & Eye Palette. With eyeshadows, blush, cheek balms, and setting powder in coordinating rose and mauve tones, this all-in-one compact takes care of most of the color decisions for you. Sweep the pale pink matte shadow all over your lids, blend a little of the deeper brown into your eyelid crease for definition, and tap the champagne shade onto the center of the lid for a hint of sparkle. Finish with a swipe of rosy blush and a little cheek balm to add dewiness. Pair the palette with the Morphe Riches Come True 5-Piece Brush & Tool Set with four makeup brushes and a mini sponge, all tucked into a metallic pouch that's easy to throw into your overnight bag.

Sources indicate that full-glam beauty invites you to play with color, whether you want a sultry smoky eye or something softer. The Charlotte Tilbury Hollywood Instant Look in a Palette offers two distinct takes on holiday glam, depending on how much drama you're going for.

Recent findings suggest that feeling a little mysterious? The Dreamy, Bronzed Beauty version features darker eyeshadows, including an especially on-trend matte burgundy, paired with a warm, sun-kissed bronzer for a moodier take on party makeup. Prefer something more delicate? Pretty, Glowing Beauty leans into pale pink tones for an ethereal, barely-there effect. Whichever you choose, blend the deeper shadow into your crease and along your lash line for definition, then tap a touch of the sparkly option onto the center of your lids to catch the light. Complete the look with the included bronzer and blush (matte or shimmery, whatever your mood), plus finishing powder to help even out your complexion. Both palettes come in glittery packaging that makes them tempting to give as gifts. (Or, you know, not.).

And because nobody wants their smoky eye turning into a smudgy mess before midnight (or after!), finish with a spritz of L'Oréal Paris Infallible 3-Second Setting Mist Spray to help keep your handiwork in place while you dance the night away.

The secret to a glowing complexion is combining finishing powders, blushes, and highlighters that deliver a healthy sheen without piling on heavy layers. If your beauty goal is less disco ball, more just-got-back-from-a-tropical-vacation, the Hourglass Ambient Lighting Edit Unlocked Palette in Wish is right up your alley.

In a recent development, the limited-edition face palette contains six powders that work together to blur the appearance of imperfections and give skin a flattering, diffused finish. Unlike chunky glitter, the finely milled formulas reflect light evenly to make your complexion look naturally radiant. For a glowy face, the versatile finishing powder doubles as powder foundation. Sweep it across your face to start, then add blush for a pop of color, and concentrate highlighter on the high points of your cheeks for a little extra definition.

If you happen to be more of a "there's no such thing as too much sparkle" person, top the look off with Fenty Beauty Limited-Edition Midnight Diamonds Diamond Bomb All-Over Diamond Veil, which leaves a fairy-dusted effect on cheekbones, collarbones, and anywhere else you want to sparkle.

The ultimate gift for the beauty chameleon includes a mix of eyeshadows, mascaras, and lip colors to create entirely different moods. For the friend who changes her makeup as often as her outfit, Tarte You Know You Love Me Collector's Set has plenty to keep her entertained.

The collection includes two mini Amazonian Clay eyeshadow palettes—one with warm golden shades and the other with cool rosy neutrals—so she can go from bronzed and sultry to pretty in pink without buying another palette. Breaking: Noah Wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 in Menswear’s Favorite Tartan

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Converse and Noah collaborated for the first time earlier this year, the most surprising thing was that it’d taken so long for them to link up.
  • Just in time for turkey season, Noah has wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 Low in one of the most beloved patterns in menswear: Black Watch tartan.
  • Recent findings suggest that in addition to the sharp Black Watch canvas uppers, Noah made a handful of other subtle changes to the classic silhouette, adding its branding to the “license plate” on the shoe’s heel, removing the wing tongue stitch, and swapping in a woven tongue tag.

When Converse and Noah collaborated for the first time earlier this year, the most surprising thing was that it’d taken so long for them to link up. The sneaker OGs and Upcoming York menswear mavens make as much sense together as peanut butter and jelly—both brands flow effortlessly between worlds, embraced by punks and preps and hoopers and skaters alike. Thankfully, the duo have been making up for lost time, kicking their partnership off with a couple of killer Chuck 70s in the spring before putting out an understated banger of a spin on the Louie Lopez 2 over the summer. Now, they’re capping off their banner year with one last go-round—another jazzed-up Chuck Taylor that’s about as holiday-ready as it gets.

Just in time for turkey season, Noah has wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 Low in one of the most beloved patterns in menswear: Black Watch tartan. The green, navy, and black plaid was originally worn by squadrons patrolling the Scottish Highlands in the 18th century, with its subdued tones meant to help wearers blend into their surroundings. Over the past several decades, it’s been embraced by fashion at large, but particularly Trad Ivy enthusiasts, who tend to sport the striking tartan on everything from sport coats and scarves during the colder months.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the sharp Black Watch canvas uppers, Noah made a handful of other subtle changes to the classic silhouette, adding its branding to the “license plate” on the shoe’s heel, removing the wing tongue stitch, and swapping in a woven tongue tag. The kicks feature the standard white laces but also come with a mustard yellow pair for an extra boost of color.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking to dress festively but aren’t all that into freaky patterned sweaters, the latest Converse x Noah Chuck 70 Low might just be the ticket. The shoes drop tomorrow, November 19, for $112 via both Converse and Noah.

Why Men Are Posting Thirst Traps in Red Light Face Masks

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gonzalo Fernández Escribano knew all about the benefits of red-light therapy for his skin.
  • "I use my red-light mask right before bed, so I’m already shirtless,” says Escribano.
  • In a recent development, escribano is one of many men online who’ve embraced the red-light thirst trap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gonzalo Fernández Escribano knew all about the benefits of red-light therapy for his skin. Fewer wrinkles, a brighter complexion, minimizing acne—he’d experienced it all firsthand when he tried out LED masks during his facials. In March 2025, he purchased one for at-home use. Little did he know it would come with an extra benefit as a provocative prop for a sexy photo.

"I use my red-light mask right before bed, so I’m already shirtless,” says Escribano. “Let’s just say the sexy-looking picture is easily convenient to take.”.

In a recent development, escribano is one of many men online who’ve embraced the red-light thirst trap. More and more, image-conscious guys with followings built around some combination of beauty, fitness, wellness, travel, are pairing their red-light routines with the occasional shirtless selfie. The trend is especially prevalent in gay-male internet culture, where faceless torsos shots, sometimes featuring beefy chests and six-pack abs, have been part of the visual language of dating apps and social media for years. A shirtless red-light-mask pic is a variation on the theme: The body and the anonymity are still there—only now there’s a skincare routine attached.

Jayson Stacy, a celebrity groomer, noticed his friend wearing an LED in his Instagram profile picture three years ago. At the same time, Stacy had recently gotten a mask himself and decided to follow suit, posting a photo of his own after Mardi Gras under the guise of some much needed recovery.

In a recent development, “It’s almost like a sexy Halloween costume, but you don’t have to wait until October,” Stacy says. Escribano agrees, saying it makes him look like a superhero. Strong shadows, glowing skin, and a Sith-like red glow mix together in a thirsty trifecta meant to slow someone’s scrolling.

For Stacy, red-light masks strike the perfect balance between wellness and plausible deniability. “You’re supposed to use the mask after you wash your face, so most are fresh out of the shower before using,” he says. “It’s like, ‘Oh, look at my morning routine,’ which gives the perfect excuse to be mostly unclothed. Then you have the mask on, you feel like someone can’t see your face, so it can feel like a layer of protection.” In other words, the skin care routine becomes the reason for the thirst trap, even though it’s only half the motivation.

Red-light therapy is a noninvasive treatment that uses low-level LED light to stimulate cellular activity and boost collagen production. The technology has become especially prominent over the last few years thanks to its ability to reduce inflammation, soften fine lines, and promote skin and muscle recovery and hair growth. (That is, as long as you are willing to invest in high-quality equipment and use it every single day).

Sources indicate that celebrities have been documenting their LED routines for years, from January Jones to Kim Kardashian. But those posts were mostly framed around the masks’ intended purpose: improving your skin. Somewhere along the way, though, a certain breed of extremely online men—trainers, models, artists, content creators, and guys who simply know their angles—found a second purpose for the masks: as an accessory for a hot photo. The masks are turning up in bathroom mirror pics, bedroom shots, and buried several slides deep in otherwise unrelated photo dumps, often without any mention of skin care at all. And judging by the comments—fire emojis, heart eyes, and the occasional “yummy”—their followers seem to be noticing something other than the mask.

The thirst traps are also surfacing on social media at a time when curiosity around red-light therapy is booming. A 2025 study analyzing Google Trends data found that search interest across red-light-therapy-related terms increased 118% after February 2024. And by 2025, Google reported that searches for “red light therapy” had reached an all-time high. As these futuristic devices have rapidly flooded our feeds, maybe it was only a matter of time before they made their way out of the skin care selfie and into something a little thirstier.

It has been revealed that in some ways these images are being ushered into well-trodden territory. In 2021, TikTok’s viral Silhouette Challenge had users transform themselves into barely distinguishable, body-forward silhouettes under a red filter, turning the color itself into a visual shorthand for sex appeal. Meanwhile, for gay men, shirtless photos are hardly a novelty, especially on dating apps like Grindr and Sniffies, where headless torsos are practically part of the experience. “The headless torsos definitely all blend together at this point,” claims John Arthur Hill, who compares swiping through hookup apps to looking into “a lukewarm batch of Chili’s skillet queso” and trying to figure out what’s cheese, meat, or a bell pepper.

Recent findings suggest that and even when the most impressive six-pack can get lost in an endless doom scroll, red light can add just enough intrigue to get someone to look twice. For Adam Pent, an OnlyFans creator who’s no stranger to posting thirst traps himself, that curiosity is part of the appeal. “It [a red-light-mask thirst trap] is definitely more interesting because I’d be curious about who’s behind the mask,” he claims. To Pent, there’s something creative about the whole thing. “I guess it makes the photo a bit more artful too? ‘Art thot’ vibes I guess, unless it looks like sponsored content.” It also makes him want to shop. “I’m less focused on the body and more like, ‘Should I just get one already?’”.

The red-light thirst trap also holds a certain mysterious appeal. “I’ve been posting ‘masked’ selfies for quite some time because I think it’s a really hot aesthetic and such a cool fantasy,” Michael Anthony, a celebrity makeup artist, notes. For him, it’s not just about looking good in the photos. “The fantasy of anonymity and pleasure, while doing something for yourself that will make you look and feel better—it’s all so sexy.”.

According to recent reports, an LED face mask is a luxurious way to get an at-home glow, and Shark's is one of our favorites. It helps to fight acne and fine lines, and it can help depuff around the eyes for those long nights.

Tattoo artist Alvin Archibald sees a similar appeal. “There’s a subtle tension between vulnerability and control that makes it interesting,” he says. “The mask takes away your facial expressions, so the body becomes the focus. It creates this interesting dynamic where you’re both exposed and concealed at the same time. There’s something almost intimate about it, like you’re getting ready for an audience without necessarily admitting it.”.

APC Just Dropped a Pair of Incredibly Clean Casios

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches.
  • The first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch.
  • That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japanese giant has just followed up its 2024 collab with APC. The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

The first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

What about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two new ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

According to recent reports, maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent fresh G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are major and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.

This story originally appeared on British GQ.

#20114. Breaking: A Newly introduced Exhibition Celebrates the Mantilla in Fashion and Art

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (661 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: A Newly introduced Exhibition Celebrates the Mantilla in Fashion and Art

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few garments have been as imitated, reinterpreted, and misunderstood as the mantilla.
  • In a recent development, “The understanding of the mantilla in all its complexity is often limited, either by a superficial reading of the symbol itself or by its association with an old-fashioned, rather conservative image of Spain,” López tells ELLE.
  • It has been revealed that the exhibition is the second installment in the Hispanic Society’s multiyear fashion initiative, which focuses on reinterpreting its own renowned collection through a new lens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few garments have been as imitated, reinterpreted, and misunderstood as the mantilla. The iconic lace veil with Spanish roots has endured for centuries. What started as an object traditionally worn for ceremonies has had a renaissance via Madonna, Rosalía, and Dolce & Gabbana, just to name a few. That’s just one of the reasons why The Hispanic Society Museum & Library in Latest York is opening its new exhibition “The Mantilla: Fashion Unveiled” beginning November 20. The museum calls the mantilla the “most distinctive garment in Spanish women’s fashion with origins dating to the 16th century.” Curated by Spanish-born scholar Carlos Usabiaga López, the show merges fashion, art, and archival material to shine a light on an iconic garment that has been donned on screen, on runways, and on red carpets for generations.

In a recent development, “The understanding of the mantilla in all its complexity is often limited, either by a superficial reading of the symbol itself or by its association with an old-fashioned, rather conservative image of Spain,” López tells ELLE. “This exhibition challenges the perception of the mantilla as an anachronistic relic of the past and reclaims its continued cultural relevance and subversive potential. From Spanish countercultural movements such as ‘La Movida Madrileña’ to drag performance, the mantilla has repeatedly been appropriated and reimagined in ways that reveal its capacity to carry newly introduced meanings.”.

It has been revealed that the exhibition is the second installment in the Hispanic Society’s multiyear fashion initiative, which focuses on reinterpreting its own renowned collection through a new lens. The museum was founded in 1903 by American philanthropist Archer Milton Huntington and has many visual examples of the garment, including Francisco Goya’s famed portrait of María del Pilar Teresa Cayetana de Silva y Álvarez de Toledo, the 13th Duchess of Alba (1762–1802). “By bringing together works of art, fashion, and material culture, the iconography of the mantilla activates a collection of such an extraordinary diversity, through unexpected dialogues between the museum’s different departments and international loans,” adds López.

The new exhibition pulls from many cultural moments new and old, including the “Spanish Craze,” which was a period of cultural fascination with Spain in the United States spanning 1890 to 1930. “During this period, the mantilla became part of a highly recognizable visual language through which Spain was imagined and represented in America,” indicates López. “Spanish performers who travelled to the United States achieved remarkable success: Raquel Meller, for instance, appeared on the cover of Time magazine in 1926, while Concha Piquer starred in From Far Seville (1923).” He also points to the reinterpretation of the mantilla in The Devil Is a Woman (1935), starring Marlene Dietrich.

Fashion naturally plays a role in the show, especially through the imagination of emerging designers, like Arturo Obegero. “Throughout the history of fashion, major designers such as Cristóbal Balenciaga and Óscar de la Renta have drawn inspiration from this [Spanish] visual language, including the mantilla,” adds López. “However, it was a curatorial decision to bring contemporary designers, including emerging voices, into direct conversation with the masterpieces in order to make justice to the mantilla’s enduring influence on fashion to this day.”.

In a recent development, the mantilla has been loved (and reinvented) in contemporary fashion at least since the 1940s, when it appeared in numerous fashion magazines. Today, the references are endless and people of all cultures and backgrounds are embracing it. “I think there is something particularly beautiful about the fact that those who have historically been excluded from the dominant narrative, who may have felt unrepresented or even oppressed by these national symbols, can now feel encouraged to revisit this folklore and expand its boundaries to make room for others to do the same,” claims López. As the exhibition makes clear, the mantilla’s compelling story is still unfolding.

“The Mantilla: Fashion Unveiled” is on view at The Hispanic Society Museum & Library from Nov. 20, 2026, through March 28, 2027.

#20111. Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1379 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart.
  • According to recent reports, as soon as the volunteer says “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over.
  • According to recent reports, the challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart. Music booms over the speakers and other competitors shuffle around the cavernous room of the Armory Track in Washington Heights, Fresh York, but Krepack stays laser-focused, thanks to years of meditation practice.

According to recent reports, as soon as the volunteer says “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over. As he lands on the other side, he sprints to the beam, dropping down into an army crawl. “Take your time, take your time,” his son yells from the sidelines. Krepack reaches the far end, rushes back, and repeats the sequence again before crossing the line in 51 seconds. To cool down, he paces back and forth with his hands on his head. “I think I’m a sprinter, I’m a jumper, but then it’s like, fuck, no, I’m 73 years old,” he says, catching his breath.

According to recent reports, the challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging. On November 7th, the inaugural day-long event drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries, and about 70% of participants were between the ages of 40 and 64. Krepeck agreed to let me shadow him to understand this new event through the lens of someone who is, in fact, aging, and would like to do so gracefully.

Sources indicate that the name of the Games comes from a buzzword that originated in the longevity world: super ager. The term was originally coined by Northwestern University researchers to describe adults over 80 whose memories rival those of people 30 years younger. These days it’s thrown around on podcasts and in books to describe anyone who defies both the typical trajectory of both cognitive and physical aging.

The inaugural Super Age Games drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries.

Sources indicate that from crawling across a cargo net to reading microexpressions, the challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill. At the end, athletes see where they rank among their age group and receive their “Super Age,” learning how their body’s physical fitness stacks up against the general U.S. population’s.

Recent findings suggest that in an era where your average middle-aged midwestern dad is training for Hyrox, and a new, outlandishly extreme challenge is being invented every few months, the Super Age games are a low-key counterpoint to raw, stunty, athleticism, born from the metric-obsessed fitness subcultures who prize longevity above all. And now that fitness trackers like Whoop or Apple Watch can track VO2max, heart rate variability, and resting heart rates, that group continues to grow. Along the way, these stats have become status symbols on par with owning a Lamborghini. And now that overall health is quantifiable, fitness values have become less about just how fast you run or how much you lift, but how slowly aging.

According to recent reports, it follows that, despite its name, Super Age Games isn’t just for aging athletes. The crowd there leaned middle-aged, and the youngest person at the competition was 21. As we stood by the dead hang station, Krepak pointed across the room at a brolic young man who looked like he could be an NFL prospect: “That dude’s a serious athlete,” he notes, as we watched him run around the track cradling a sandbag on his shoulder.

In a recent development, unlike competitions like Hyrox, where athletes race through a sequence of workouts against the clock, the Super Age Games allows competitors to rest as long as they need between trials. In fact, Junior Kennedy, the fitness program director for the Games, encourages it. “There's no rush,” he claims. “The goal is to get through each event as intentionally as you can. We need to understand what it means to recover.”.

Each trial was developed with a certain longevity marker in mind, and developed with input from researchers at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, a leading nonprofit research center based in Novato, California dedicated to understanding aging. The Over Under, for example, tests agility by judging how fast you can change levels and switch directions. Meanwhile, the Synapse, a challenge where participants track moving balls on a screen and identify them after they've been shuffled around, is meant to measure cognitive processing.

Challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill.

Krepack, a psychologist and lifelong athlete from Mill Valley, California, first heard about the event through its founder, David Stewart. Stewart is a media founder behind two niche longevity platforms, AGEIST and Super Age, where he writes about longevity, wellness, and redefining aging (one of his website testimonial’s says he has made aging “cool and aspirational.”). Krepack’s generally a skeptic of the profit-driven modern wellness industry—“I've always had a jaded view of all of that stuff,” he says—but he has followed both Stewart and the Buck Institutes’ work for years.

The competition appealed to Krepack, in part because he’s spent decades cultivating a consistent exercise routine he’s proud of. He played baseball in college and has spent much of his life skiing, cycling, and playing other sports. These days, his schedule revolves around a handful of rituals: bike rides on Mondays and Fridays, a Saturday hike with a friend, gardening, yoga, and Zen meditation most days. When he signed up for the Games in June, he altered his exercise routine, lifted more weights, practiced hanging from a bar, and experimented with the Neurotracker cognitive test online.

It has been revealed that yet all that training didn’t prepare Krepack for the biggest surprise of his day. After scoring well on both the Inferno (the assault bike VO2max test) and Synapse, next came the fourth trial: the “Tightrope,” a balance challenge that requires competitors to walk along a low beam while carrying a water-filled bag, taking as many consecutive steps as they can in two minutes without falling. He had expected to excel, thanks to years of skiing and yoga. Instead, he struggled to keep steady as the water shifted inside the bag. As his foot slipped off the bar, his eyes got wide. “I can’t believe my balance,” he indicates. “That’s my one disappointment in life now.”.

Alan Krepack's sons Harrison and Aaron during the “tightrope” challenge.

According to recent reports, krepack was still hard on himself as we walked over to the dead hang trial. But after beating both his sons’ times, he seemed to get his competitive spirit back. He pushed through the remaining challenge determined to finish strong. And he did: By the end of the Games, he had placed second overall, with scores adjusted for age.

Sources indicate that A few days after the competition, I checked in with Krepack to ask him how he’d processed the event. He responded with screenshots of his scores. His highest score came from the cargo net, which he credited to sheer determination rather than any particular finesse: “due to my will and overcoming an unconventional and desperate style!” he texted me, “Plus my sons were great support and focus partners.”.

Industry observers note that but the Games were also a reality check about aging: “I left there feeling both young and old,” he tells me on a phone call. As he watched his sons rocket through the obstacles, he was forced to confront how much of his athleticism he’d lost. “They just flew over it. They were so fluid, and so fast,” he states. “I’m not 30 or 40 or 50 or 60 anymore.”.

Despite all the longevity industry's promises of maintaining youth, Krepack sees little value in denying the inevitable. Aging well, he says, is about “accepting, improving, and doing your best. It’s not a denial of who you are at this point in life.” The goal, he says, is to make the most of what you’re still capable of.

#20106. Pride and Prejudice’s Rufus Sewell Is the Most Dashing Man on Television

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1572 w)
